Federal Reserve Board releases results of supplemental stress test

Published 2026-10-06 14:30 UTC

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday released the results of a supplemental stress test that examined how large banks would fare under a set of additional hypothetical scenarios. All participating banks remained above their minimum capital requirements under each scenario.

The supplemental exercise was separate from the annual stress test and was designed to explore a wider range of risks. It included a scenario with a sharp rise in long-term interest rates combined with a decline in commercial real estate prices, and a second scenario featuring the simultaneous failure of five large hedge funds that are counterparties to the banks.

Under the interest rate scenario, aggregate common equity capital ratios declined by 2.4 percentage points at their lowest point, compared with a decline of 2.8 percentage points in the annual test. Losses on commercial real estate loans were concentrated in office properties, where the scenario assumed price declines of 40 percent.

In the counterparty scenario, banks with large trading businesses would lose between $70 billion and $85 billion in total, depending on the assumptions about how quickly positions could be closed. The Board said the results show that banks' risk management of their exposures to nonbank financial institutions has improved, though concentrations remain in some areas.

The supplemental results will not be used to set capital requirements. The Board said the exercise is intended to inform supervisors and the public about vulnerabilities that the annual test may not capture, and it plans to run similar exploratory analyses in future years.

Detailed results for each participating firm, along with a description of the methodology, are available on the Board's website. The Board will host a briefing for analysts next week to answer questions about the design of the scenarios.

The Board noted that the supplemental scenarios are not forecasts and were chosen to be severe. Banks did not have to submit capital plans based on the results, and no firm will face changes to its stress capital buffer as a result of the exercise.
